content.rendered:
THE 68.25 per cent collapse in Company Income Tax payments by Nigeria’s manufacturing sector in the first quarter of 2026 should alarm policymakers far beyond the tax authorities. The plunge from N234.59 billion in Q1 2025 to N74.48 billion in Q1 2026 is a clear signal that the country’s productive base is under severe stress. Obviously, manufacturers need a lifeline.

Manufacturing remains the backbone of every successful economy. It creates jobs at scale, stimulates agricultural demand, supports logistics and services, generates exports, develops technological capability and expands the tax base. When factories struggle, the entire economy eventually feels the pain.

The latest NBS figures indicate that manufacturing tax payments fell by N160.11 billion year-on-year and by 47.49 per cent compared with the previous quarter.

While total CIT collections declined by 31.05 per cent nationally, the manufacturing sector experienced a much sharper contraction, suggesting that the real economy is bearing the heaviest burden of Nigeria’s difficult economic transition.

The decline comes at a particularly delicate period. The implementation of the new tax framework, including the reduction of CIT from 30 per cent to 25 per cent, coincided with worsening operational conditions for producers. The result is a combination of lower tax rates and significantly lower corporate profitability.

Supporters of the tax reforms argue that lower rates should ultimately stimulate investment and improve business survival.

The Chairman of the Presidential Fiscal Policy and Tax Reforms Committee and current Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, has consistently defended the reforms as a major relief package for businesses.

According to him, reducing corporate income tax by five percentage points effectively leaves about N1.4 trillion in the hands of businesses annually.

The new laws also introduced zero per cent CIT for smaller firms and expanded tax exemptions for businesses with annual turnover below N50 million. The objective is to reduce the tax burden, improve compliance and allow firms to retain more capital for expansion. This is commendable.

However, lower tax rates mean little if companies have little or no profit to tax.

The CIT is fundamentally a profit tax. If profits collapse, tax collections inevitably fall. The latest figures, therefore, reveal not only the impact of tax reforms but the deteriorating health of the manufacturing sector itself.

Manufacturers continue to grapple with some of the highest operating costs in Africa.

Energy remains perhaps the biggest challenge. Unreliable grid power forces firms to rely heavily on diesel generators, while electricity tariffs have risen substantially.

Fuel prices remain elevated, transport costs have surged, and logistics bottlenecks continue to inflate operating expenses.

Foreign exchange shocks have compounded these pressures. The Manufacturers Association of Nigeria has repeatedly warned that exchange-rate liberalisation has generated enormous forex losses and increased production costs running into trillions of naira, especially for firms dependent on imported machinery, raw materials and industrial inputs.

Data from MAN’s CEO Confidence Index showed that nearly 49 per cent of manufacturers’ foreign exchange requirements are still unmet through official channels, forcing a resort to costlier alternative sources, further shrinking already thin profit margins.

The cost of borrowing has become equally debilitating. Commercial lending rates exceeding 30 to 35 per cent make expansion financing virtually impossible for many manufacturers. Few industries can borrow at such rates and remain profitable.

Weak consumer demand further compounds the crisis. Inflation has severely eroded household purchasing power, leaving many manufacturers with rising inventories that reached a record N1.8 trillion as of Q3 2025 amid declining sales volumes.

Consequently, firms face the worst of both worlds in soaring costs and weak demand.

This explains why manufacturing, despite contributing 13.82 per cent of domestic CIT and remaining the country’s third-largest domestic tax contributor, now accounts for only about 5.45 per cent of total national CIT collections.

Indeed, foreign tax payments contributed N828.82 billion, representing 60.6 per cent of total collections in Q1 2026, while domestic sectors increasingly struggle.

The implications extend beyond tax revenue, as manufacturing is one of Nigeria’s largest potential employers. Every factory job creates additional employment opportunities in transportation, agriculture, retail, maintenance and services.

Industrial growth remains essential for reducing unemployment, expanding exports and reducing excessive dependence on crude oil revenues.

Economic analysts have progressively expressed concern that the productive economy is being overshadowed by sectors that generate revenue without necessarily creating large-scale employment.

Analysts at SBM Intelligence have argued that while statutory tax rates may be falling, businesses continue to face multiple levies, compliance costs and emerging obligations that may offset some of the intended benefits of tax reductions.

Therefore, the government must complement fiscal reforms with aggressive industrial support policies.

For starters, energy costs must be addressed. Dedicated industrial power schemes, gas-to-power incentives and embedded generation arrangements for industrial clusters should receive urgent attention. Reliable electricity would significantly reduce production costs.

Affordable financing must become a priority, with intervention funds through the Bank of Industry and development finance institutions expanded at single-digit interest rates to support working capital, equipment acquisition, and expansion.

Beyond pronouncements, tax harmonisation must be vigorously implemented. Manufacturers frequently complain about multiple taxation across federal, state and local governments. Eliminating overlapping levies would improve the ease of doing business.

Also, foreign exchange stability, which appears almost achieved, must be maintained.

Manufacturers require predictable exchange rates for planning, pricing and procurement. Greater liquidity and stability in the foreign exchange market would reduce uncertainty and protect margins.

Government procurement policies should intentionally prioritise locally manufactured products wherever possible. Strong local demand can help factories achieve economies of scale and improve profitability.

Crucially, infrastructure investments in roads, ports and logistics corridors will lower logistics costs that directly translate into higher productivity and competitiveness.

Despite the Bola Tinubu administration’s aggressive revenue drive, Nigeria cannot tax industries into prosperity, and neither can it expect strong tax revenues from struggling manufacturers.

Sustainable tax growth depends on profitable businesses, expanding production and rising investment.

If Nigeria genuinely seeks inclusive growth, mass employment and durable revenues, supporting manufacturing is not optional. The productive sector remains the engine of the real economy. Reviving it is perhaps the most important economic task facing policymakers today.
